Polynomial harmonic morphisms and eigenfamilies on spheres

Oskar Riedler
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The eigenfamilies of Gudmundsson and Sakovich [12] can be used to generate harmonic morphisms, proper rr-harmonic maps, and minimal co-dimension 22 submanifolds. This article begins by characterising the globally defined eigenfamilies of the sphere SmS^{m}; they correspond to orthogonal families of homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms from ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1} to ℂ\mathds{C}, all of the same degree. We investigate and construct such families, paying special attention to those that are not congruent to families of holomorphic polynomials. Strong restrictions for families of such polynomials are found in low dimensions, and the pairs of degree 22 maps that induce an eigenfamily are classified.

1 Introduction

Let (M,g),(N,h)(M,g),(N,h) be two Riemannian manifolds. A harmonic morphism is a smooth map φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N that pulls back germs of harmonic maps on NN to germs of harmonic maps on MM, i.e. for all (locally defined) harmonic maps f:U⊆N→ℝf:U\subseteq N\to\mathds{R} one has that f∘φ:φ−1​(U)⊆M→ℝf\circ\varphi:\varphi^{-1}(U)\subseteq M\to\mathds{R} is harmonic. The theory of harmonic morphisms between Riemannian manifolds begins with the works of Fuglede [8] and Ishihara [15], who found a geometric characterisation of the above condition: A map φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N is a harmonic morphism if and only if it is harmonic and weakly horizontally conformal.

The case dim(N)=2\dim(N)=2 is especially interesting for two reasons. First the level sets φ−1​({y})∩(M∖S)\varphi^{-1}(\{y\})\cap(M\setminus S) are then minimal submanifolds of M∖SM\setminus S (here S={x∈M∣Dx​φ=0}S=\{x\in M\mid D_{x}\varphi=0\} denotes the singular points of φ\varphi ), and one obtains a codimension 22 foliation of M∖SM\setminus S consisting of minimal submanifolds, c.f. [2]. Secondly the property of φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N being a harmonic morphism is in this case invariant under conformal changes of the metric on NN. So one can always assume, at least locally, that the codomain is ℂ\mathds{C} with its Euclidean metric.

For maps with codomain ℂ\mathds{C} the conditions of being harmonic and weakly horizontally conformal can be expressed by simple equations. A map φ:M→ℂ\varphi:M\to\mathds{C} is a harmonic morphism if and only if (see e.g. [5]):

Δ​φ=0,\displaystyle\Delta\varphi=0, (1)
gℂ​(∇φ,∇φ)=0.\displaystyle g_{\mathds{C}}(\nabla\varphi,\nabla\varphi)=0. (2)

Here ∇φ\nabla\varphi is the section of T​M⊗ℂTM\otimes\mathds{C} given by ∇Re(φ)+i∇Im(φ)\nabla\mathrm{Re}(\varphi)+i\nabla\mathrm{Im}(\varphi) and gℂg_{\mathds{C}} denotes the complex bilinear extension of the metric gg to T​M⊗ℂTM\otimes\mathds{C}.

Equations (1) and (2) form and overdetermined system of partial differential equations, so a priori it is not clear if any solutions exist. In fact Baird and Wood [4] have shown that the 3-dimensional homogeneous space Sol\mathrm{Sol} does not even admit any locally defined harmonic morphisms to ℂ\mathds{C}.

Motivated by the existence problem of harmonic morphisms, Gudmundsson and Sakovich [12] introduced the notion of an eigenfamily, which can be used to generate families of harmonic morphisms:

Definition 1.1.

Let λ,μ∈ℂ\lambda,\mu\in\mathds{C}. A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of smooth functions from MM to ℂ\mathds{C} is called a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on MM if for all φ,ψ∈ℱ\varphi,\psi\in\mathcal{F}:

Δ​φ=λ​φ,\displaystyle\Delta\varphi=\lambda\varphi, (3)
gℂ​(∇φ,∇ψ)=μ​φ​ψ.\displaystyle g_{\mathds{C}}(\nabla\varphi,\nabla\psi)=\mu\,\varphi\psi. (4)

Functions that are elements of some (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily are called (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfunctions.

Remark.

Comparing with equations (1), (2) one notes that a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfunction is the same as a complex valued harmonic morphism.

Theorem (Gudmundsson-Sakovich, c.f. Theorem 2.5 in [12]).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on MM, then for any φ1,…,φk∈ℱ\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k}\in\mathcal{F} and homogeneous polynomials P,Q∈ℂ⁡[z1,…,zk]P,Q\in\mathds{C}[z_{1},...,z_{k}] of the same degree, the map P∘(φ1,…,φk)Q∘(φ1,…,φk)\dfrac{P\circ(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k})}{Q\circ(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k})} is a harmonic morphism on M∖{x∈M∣Q⁡(φ1​(x),…,φk​(x))=0}M\setminus\{x\in M\mid Q(\varphi_{1}(x),...,\varphi_{k}(x))=0\}.

In a series of papers [12, 13, 9] Gudmundsson and co-authors construct eigenfamilies on each of the classical compact symmetric spaces. A duality principle induces eigenfamilies on the non-compact duals of these spaces. In this way they explicitly construct for many symmetric spaces the first known examples of harmonic morphisms.

In addition to their use in generating harmonic morphisms, it was shown by Gudmundsson and Sobak [14] that eigenfunctions can be used to explicitly construct proper rr-harmonic maps with an open dense domain, and Gudmundsson and Munn [11] use them to construct minimal submanifolds of co-dimension 22.

In this article we begin by considering eigenfamilies on the sphere SmS^{m} with global domain. It is a simple observation that such families are in bijection with (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies on ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1} consisting of homogeneous polynomials all of the same degree.

Theorem 1.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of maps from SmS^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}, and λ,μ∈ℂ\lambda,\mu\in\mathds{C}. The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamliy.

  2. (ii)

    There is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily ℱ~\widetilde{\mathcal{F}} of homogeneous polynomials from ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1} to ℂ\mathds{C}, all of the same degree dd, so that the map

    ℱ~→ℱ,F↦F|Sm,\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\to\mathcal{F},\qquad F\mapsto F\lvert_{S^{m}},

    is a well defined bijection and λ=−d⁡(d+m−1)\lambda=-d(d+m-1), μ=−d2\mu=-d^{2}.

The other compact rank one symmetric spaces, with exception of the Cayley plane, can be obtained from the sphere via a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibres. One then gets a characterisation of the global eigenfamilies on the real, complex, and quaternionic projective spaces:

Theorem 2.

Let X∈{ℝ​ℙm,ℂ​ℙm,ℍ​ℙm}X\in\{\mathds{RP}^{m},\mathds{CP}^{m},\mathds{HP}^{m}\} and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a family of functions on XX to ℂ\mathds{C}. Denoting with π:Sm⁡(X)→X\pi:S^{m(X)}\to X the usual submersion one has that the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on XX.

  2. (ii)

    π∗(ℱ)={F∘π:Sm⁡(X)→ℂ∣F∈ℱ}\pi^{*}(\mathcal{F})=\{F\circ\pi:S^{m(X)}\to\mathds{C}\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on Sm⁡(X)S^{m(X)}.

The rest of the article then concerns (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies on ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1} consisting of homogeneous polynomials of the same degree. The elements of such an eigenfamily are homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms, which are objects of independent interest and have been studied in the past (see e.g. [1] and [5]). Note that if a family of polynomials is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily then clearly (λ,μ)=(0,0)(\lambda,\mu)=(0,0), so we will refer to (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies simply as eigenfamilies when dealing with polynomials.

Families of holomorphic maps ℂm→ℂ\mathds{C}^{m}\to\mathds{C} are automatically (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies. In particular the space of holomorphic homogeneous polynomials of degree dd provides an immediate example of a polynomial eigenfamily; that these induce eigenfamilies on the sphere is known (see [11]). The question of finding families that are not holomorphic with respect to any Kähler structure then arises naturally. The following definition is a convenient way of encoding holomorphy of functions (also on odd dimensional ℝm\mathds{R}^{m}), without referencing any fixed Kähler structure:

Definition 1.2.
  1. 1.

    A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions from ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} said to be uniformly of complex type if there is a k≥0k\geq 0, an orthogonal projection π:ℝm→ℂk\pi:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}^{k}, and a family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of holomorphic maps ℂk→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\to\mathds{C} so that ℱ=π∗​(𝒢):={G∘π∣G∈𝒢}\mathcal{F}=\pi^{*}(\mathcal{G})\vcentcolon=\{G\circ\pi\mid G\in\mathcal{G}\}.

  2. 2.

    A function F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is said to be of complex type if the family {F}\{F\} is uniformly of complex type.

By work of Baird and Wood [3] and Wood [19] it is well known that any globally defined harmonic morphism ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} for m≤4m\leq 4 is of complex type. This remains true in the context of (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies:

Theorem 4.

Let m≤4m\leq 4 and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily of maps (not necessarily polynomials) ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type.

There is a very simple criterion with which one can determine when a function or family is of complex type:

Theorem 3.

A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of smooth functions from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C} is uniformly of complex type if and only if the gradients {∇xF∣x∈ℝm,F∈ℱ}\{\nabla_{\!x}F\mid x\in\mathds{R}^{m},F\in\mathcal{F}\} span an isotropic subspace of ℝm⊗ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\otimes\mathds{C}, i.e. if and only if for all F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} and x,y∈ℝmx,y\in\mathds{R}^{m}:

(∇xF)T​∇yG=0.(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!y}G=0. (5)

We expect this result to be known. But since we do not have a reference for this characterisation, a proof is included in Section 3 for convenience of the reader. It is interesting to note that for a homogeneous degree 22 polynomial ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}, x↦xT​A​xx\mapsto x^{T}Ax the condition of being a harmonic morphism and the condition of being of complex type coincide.

Using Theorem 3, one can check for example that the following family is an eigenfamily on ℝ8\mathds{R}^{8} consisting of degree 33 homogeneous polynomials, and that the family is not uniformly of complex type:

{ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,w,v)↦a(z2w+zuv¯)+b(zuw¯−z2v)+c(u2v¯+zuw)+d(u2w¯−zuv)∣a,b,c,d∈ℂ}.\{\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},(z,u,w,v)\mapsto a(z^{2}w+zu\overline{v})+b(zu\overline{w}-z^{2}v)+c(u^{2}\overline{v}+zuw)+d(u^{2}\overline{w}-zuv)\mid a,b,c,d\in\mathds{C}\}.

A feature of this example is that even though the maps are generically not of complex type, they are still all holomorphic in the variables z,uz,u. It turns out to be useful to encode the existence of such holomorphic variables in the notion of an axis of holomorphy (c.f. Definition 3.4). One has for instance:

Theorem 5.

Let m∈{5,6}m\in\{5,6\} and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is an eigenfamily of homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}. If ℱ\mathcal{F} has a uniform axis of holomorphy of (real) dimension at least 22, then ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type.

Eigenfamilies consisting of homogeneous degree 22 polynomials on ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} always admit a uniform axis of holomorphy of dimension at least 22:

Theorem 6.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an eigenfamily of homogeneous degree 22 polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} admits a uniform axis of holomorphy of (real) dimension at least min⁡(2,m)\min(2,m).

Leveraging the notion of an axis of holomorphy allows one to classify all pairs F1,F2F_{1},F_{2} of degree 22 homogeneous polynomials ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} for which {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} is an eigenfamily. See Definition 4.3 in Section 4 for the relevant definitions:

Theorem 7.

Let F1,F2:ℝm→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} be two homogenous degree 22 polynomials so that {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} is a full eigenfamily. Then there are subspace data (n,k,δ)(n,k,\delta) as well as polynomial and twisting data (P1,P2,A)(P_{1},P_{2},A), (Y,C,v)(Y,C,v) so that:

  1. 1.

    Up to an isometry of the domain one can decompose ℝm≅ℂn⊕ℂk⊕ℝδ\mathds{R}^{m}\cong\mathds{C}^{n}\oplus\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{\delta} so that ℂn\mathds{C}^{n} is a maximal uniform axis of holomorphy for {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\}.

  2. 2.

    Let X=(12​v​vT+C)​Y−1X=(\frac{1}{2}vv^{T}+C)Y^{-1}. One has, with respect to the above decomposition:

    F1((z1,….,zn),(w1,…,wk),t)\displaystyle F_{1}((z_{1},....,z_{n}),(w_{1},...,w_{k}),t) =P1​(z1,…,zn)+∑i​jzi​Ai​j​wj\displaystyle=P_{1}(z_{1},...,z_{n})+\sum_{ij}z_{i}A_{ij}w_{j}
    F2((z1,….,zn),(w1,…,wk),t)\displaystyle F_{2}((z_{1},....,z_{n}),(w_{1},...,w_{k}),t) =P2​(z1,…,zn)+∑i​jzi​Ai​j​(∑lXj​l​wl+∑lYj​l​w¯l+vj​t)\displaystyle=P_{2}(z_{1},...,z_{n})+\sum_{ij}z_{i}A_{ij}\left(\sum_{l}X_{jl}w_{l}+\sum_{l}Y_{jl}\overline{w}_{l}+v_{j}t\right)

Additionally for any subspace type together with polynomial and twisting data the above equations define an eigenfamily on ℝ2​(n+k)+δ\mathds{R}^{2(n+k)+\delta}.

The article ends with examples of methods with which homogeneous polynomial eigenfamilies on ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} can be constructed, see Section 5.

The article is organised as follows: In Section 2 we provide background information on harmonic morphisms and (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies, and prove Theorems 1 and 2. In Section 3 we investigate the question of when (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies are holomorphic, here we define the notions of complex type and that of an axis of holomorphy and provide examples of eigenfamilies that are not of complex type. Theorems 3, 4, 5 are proven in this section, and we describe how an axis of holomorphy leads to a reduction principle (c.f. Proposition 3.10). In Section 4 we investigate the case of eigenfamilies consisting of degree 22 polynomials, showing Theorems 6 and 7. Finally Section 5 reviews some constructions.

2 Eigenfamilies on spheres

In subsection 2.1 we review some basic facts about harmonic morphisms and (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies. In subsection 2.2 we show Theorem 1 and we show Theorem 2 in subsection 2.3.

For an overview of the theory and history of harmonic morphisms we recommend both the book [5] and the regularly updated online bibliography [10].

2.1 Harmonic morphisms and (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies

Let (M,g)(M,g), (N,h)(N,h) be two Riemannian manifolds.

Definition 2.1.

A smooth map map φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N is called a harmonic morphism if for every U⊆NU\subseteq N open and f:U→ℝf:U\to\mathds{R} harmonic the composition f∘φ:φ−1​(U)→ℝf\circ\varphi:\varphi^{-1}(U)\to\mathds{R} is again harmonic.

These maps were originally studied in the context of Brelot harmonic spaces and potential theory. The geometric theory begins with the work of Fuglede and Ishihara, who independently found an infinitesimal characterisation of the above definition on Riemannian manifolds:

Theorem (Fuglede [8], Ishihara [15]).

A smooth map φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N is a harmonic morphism if and only if its harmonic and weakly horizontally conformal.

We briefly explain these conditions:

Definition 2.2.
  1. 1.

    A smooth map between two Riemannian manifolds (M,g)(M,g) and (N,h)(N,h) is called harmonic if it is a stationary point of the energy functional φ↦∫M‖D​φ‖2\varphi\mapsto\int_{M}\|D\varphi\|^{2}.

  2. 2.

    A smooth map φ:(M,g)→(N,h)\varphi:(M,g)\to(N,h) is called weakly horizontally conformal if at any point x∈Mx\in M the differential Dx​φD_{x}\varphi is either 00 or it maps the horizontal space ker⁡(Dx​φ)⟂⊂Tx​M\ker(D_{x}\varphi)^{\perp}\subset T_{x}M conformally onto Tφ⁡(x)​NT_{\varphi(x)}N.

Remark.
  1. 1.

    φ:(M,g)→(N,h)\varphi:(M,g)\to(N,h) is harmonic if and only if the tension field τ(φ)=Tr(∇Dφ)\tau(\varphi)=\Tr(\nabla D\varphi) vanishes.

  2. 2.

    If φ:(M,g)→(N,h)\varphi:(M,g)\to(N,h) is weakly horizontally conformal there exists a function λ:M→ℝ\lambda:M\to\mathds{R}, called the conformality factor, so that φ∗(h)=λ2g|ker⁡(d​φ)⟂\varphi^{*}(h)=\lambda^{2}g\lvert_{\ker(d\varphi)^{\perp}}, meaning that for all x∈Mx\in M, v,w∈ker⁡(Dx​φ)⟂⊂Tx​Mv,w\in\ker(D_{x}\varphi)^{\perp}\subset T_{x}M one has:

    h⁡(Dx​φ​v,Dx​φ​w)=λ2​(x)​g​(v,w).h(D_{x}\varphi\,v,D_{x}\varphi\,w)=\lambda^{2}(x)\,g(v,w).

The theory of harmonic morphisms between Riemannian manifolds is extremely rich, we will only briefly remark on two aspects. First one has that homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms between vector spaces arise naturally:

Theorem (Fuglede [8]).

Let φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N be a harmonic morphism and suppose x∈Mx\in M is a critical point of φ\varphi. Then xx is of finite order and the symbol of φ\varphi at xx is a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism between the real vector spaces Tx​M→Tφ⁡(x)​NT_{x}M\to T_{\varphi(x)}N.

Secondly there is a strong connection with minimal submanifolds, in the case dim(N)=2\dim(N)=2 this connection is especially strong and is expressed by the following statement:

Theorem (Baird-Eells [2]).

Suppose φ:M→N\varphi:M\to N is horizontally weakly conformal and dim(N)=2\dim(N)=2, then φ\varphi is harmonic (and so a harmonic morphism) if and only if the fibres of φ\varphi are minimal at regular points.

In the case that dim(N)=2\dim(N)=2 one notes that the property of being a harmonic morphism is preserved under conformal transformations of the codomain. In particular if dim(N)=2\dim(N)=2 the problem of local existence of harmonic morphisms M→NM\to N is captured entirely by the case N=ℂN=\mathds{C} equipped with its Euclidean metric. A calculation shows that a map φ:M→ℂ\varphi:M\to\mathds{C} is a harmonic morphism if and only if (see e.g. [8]):

Δ​φ=0,gℂ​(∇φ,∇φ)=0.\Delta\varphi=0,\qquad g_{\mathds{C}}(\nabla\varphi,\nabla\varphi)=0.

Here Δ\Delta denotes the Laplacian of (M,g)(M,g), gℂg_{\mathds{C}} is the complex bilinear extension of gg to T​M⊗ℂTM\otimes\mathds{C}, and ∇φ:M→T​M⊗ℂ\nabla\varphi:M\to TM\otimes\mathds{C} is the map ∇Re(φ)+i∇Im(φ)\nabla\mathrm{Re}(\varphi)+i\,\nabla\mathrm{Im}(\varphi).

We now turn to eigenfamilies. It is often convenient to refer to the conformality operator in this context:

Definition 2.3.

The conformality operator κ:C∞​(M,ℂ)×C∞​(M,ℂ)→C∞​(M,ℂ)\kappa:C^{\infty}(M;\mathds{C})\times C^{\infty}(M;\mathds{C})\to C^{\infty}(M;\mathds{C}) is defined by κ⁡(φ,ψ)=gℂ​(∇φ,∇ψ)\kappa(\varphi,\psi)=g_{\mathds{C}}(\nabla\varphi,\nabla\psi).

A map φ:M→ℂ\varphi:M\to\mathds{C} is then weakly horizontally conformal if and only if κ⁡(φ,φ)=0\kappa(\varphi,\varphi)=0. Recall the definition of a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily from the introduction:

Definition 2.4 (Gudmundsson-Sakovich [12]).

Let λ,μ∈ℂ\lambda,\mu\in\mathds{C}. A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of smooth functions from MM to ℂ\mathds{C} is called a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily if for all φ,ψ∈ℱ\varphi,\psi\in\mathcal{F}:

Δ​φ=λ​φ,κ⁡(φ,ψ)=μ​φ​ψ.\Delta\varphi=\lambda\varphi,\qquad\kappa(\varphi,\psi)=\mu\varphi\psi.

Functions that are elements of some (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily are called (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfunctions.

As explained in the introduction, eigenfamilies can provide a wealth of harmonic morphisms [12], proper rr-harmonic maps [14], and mininal submanifold of codimension 2 [11].

It is useful to note that the property of being an eigenfamily is closed under taking powers:

Remark.

If ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily and d∈ℕd\in\mathds{N}, then

ℱd:=spanℂ{φ1⋯φd∣φi∈ℱ}\mathcal{F}^{d}\vcentcolon=\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{\varphi_{1}\cdots\varphi_{d}\mid\varphi_{i}\in\mathcal{F}\}

is a (λ~,μ~)(\widetilde{\lambda},\widetilde{\mu})-eigenfamily, where λ~=d⁡(λ+(d−1)​μ)\widetilde{\lambda}=d(\lambda+(d-1)\mu) and μ~=d2​μ\widetilde{\mu}=d^{2}\mu. See e.g. Lemma A.1 in [12].

2.2 Eigenfamilies on SmS^{m}

We now show the first result of this article, which is a characterisation of the globally defined eigenfamilies on the spheres SmS^{m}.

Theorem 1.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of maps from SmS^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}, and λ,μ∈ℂ\lambda,\mu\in\mathds{C}. The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamliy.

  2. (ii)

    There is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily ℱ~\widetilde{\mathcal{F}} of homogeneous polynomials from ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1} to ℂ\mathds{C}, all of the same degree dd, so that the map

    ℱ~→ℱ,F↦F|Sm,\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\to\mathcal{F},\qquad F\mapsto F\lvert_{S^{m}},

    is a well defined bijection and λ=−d⁡(d+m−1)\lambda=-d(d+m-1), μ=−d2\mu=-d^{2}.

Proof.

Before beginning with the proof note that if F:ℝm+1→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m+1}\to\mathds{C} is homogeneous of degree dd one then has for all x∈ℝm+1x\in\mathds{R}^{m+1}, x≠0x\neq 0:

∇xℝm+1F=d⋅F(x)x‖x‖2+∥x∥d−1∇x/‖x‖Sm(F|Sm).\nabla_{\!x}^{\mathds{R}^{m+1}}F=d\cdot F(x)\frac{x}{\|x\|^{2}}+\|x\|^{d-1}\nabla_{\!x/\|x\|}^{S^{m}}(F\lvert_{S^{m}}). (6)

Here we use ∇xM​F\nabla_{\!x}^{M}F to denote the gradient in a Riemannian manifold MM of a function F:M→ℂF:M\to\mathds{C} at a point x∈Mx\in M.

Starting with (i)⟹\implies(ii):

A globally defined map f:Sm→ℂf:S^{m}\to\mathds{C} satisfies Δ​f=λ​f\Delta f=\lambda f for some λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathds{C}, i.e. is an eigenfunction of the Laplacian, if and only if it is a spherical harmonic, i.e. there is a homogenous harmonic polynomial F:ℝm+1→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m+1}\to\mathds{C} such that F|Sm=fF\lvert_{S^{m}}=f. The homogeneous polynomial FF is uniquely determined, denoting its degree by dd one has λ=−d⁡(d+m−1)\lambda=-d(d+m-1), see e.g. Chapter III.C.1 of [6] for a textbook treatment.

For a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions Sm→ℂS^{m}\to\mathds{C} one then defines:

ℱ~:={F∈ℂ[x1,…,xm+1]∣F homogeneous,ΔF=0,F|Sm∈ℱ}.\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\vcentcolon=\{F\in\mathds{C}[x_{1},...,x_{m+1}]\mid F\text{ homogeneous},\Delta F=0,F\lvert_{S^{m}}\in\mathcal{F}\}.

In particular λ=−d⁡(d+m−1)\lambda=-d(d+m-1), where dd is the degree of the elements of ℱ~\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}, and the map ℱ~→ℱ\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\to\mathcal{F} induced by the restriction to SmS^{m} is a bijection.

From Theorem 2.1 of [1] it is known that a weakly horizontally conformal map ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} for which each component is a polynomial is automatically harmonic. In our case this gives the following simplification:

Corollary 2.5.

A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of polynomials ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily on ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} if and only if for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathds{R}^{m} and F1,F2∈ℱF_{1},F_{2}\in\mathcal{F}:

(∇xF1)T​∇xF2=0.(\nabla_{\!x}F_{1})^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}F_{2}=0.

(∇xF)T​∇xF=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}F=0 (7)

holds for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathds{R}^{m}.

2.3 Other compact rank one symmetric spaces

Theorem 2.

Let X∈{ℝ​ℙm,ℂ​ℙm,ℍ​ℙm}X\in\{\mathds{RP}^{m},\mathds{CP}^{m},\mathds{HP}^{m}\} and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a family of functions on XX to ℂ\mathds{C}. Denoting with π:Sm⁡(X)→X\pi:S^{m(X)}\to X the usual submersion one has that the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on XX.

  2. (ii)

    π∗(ℱ)={F∘π:Sm⁡(X)→ℂ∣F∈ℱ}\pi^{*}(\mathcal{F})=\{F\circ\pi:S^{m(X)}\to\mathds{C}\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\} is a (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamily on Sm⁡(X)S^{m(X)}.

Proof.

In each of the above cases the map π:Sm⁡(X)→X\pi:S^{m(X)}\to X is a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibres. For any F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} this then implies:

κX​(F,G)∘π=κSm⁡(X)​(F∘π,G∘π),(ΔX​F)∘π=ΔSm⁡(X)​(F∘π).\kappa_{X}(F,G)\circ\pi=\kappa_{S^{m(X)}}(F\circ\pi,G\circ\pi),\qquad(\Delta_{X}F)\circ\pi=\Delta_{S^{m(X)}}(F\circ\pi).

The statement then follows immediately. ∎

Together with Theorem 1 this characterises the globally defined eigenfamilies on compact rank one symmetric spaces, with exception of the Cayley plane 𝕆​ℙ2\mathds{OP}^{2}, in terms of families of polynomial harmonic morphisms. In each case the families that descend to eigenfamilies on the symmetric space are precisely those consisting of GG-invariant polynomials. Here G∈{S0,S1,S3}G\in\{S^{0},S^{1},S^{3}\} depending on whether XX is a real, complex, or quaternionic projective space.

Example 2.6.
  1. 1.

    If X=ℝ​ℙmX=\mathds{RP}^{m} then (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies correspond to eigenfamilies of homogeneous {±1}\{\pm 1\}-invariant complex valued polynomials on ℝm+1\mathds{R}^{m+1}. The condition of {±1}\{\pm 1\}-invariance means that the polynomials must be of even degree. The range of values (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu) for which there exist global (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies is {(−2​d​(m−1+2​d),−4​d2)∣d∈ℕ}\{(-2d(m-1+2d),-4d^{2})\mid d\in\mathds{N}\}.

  2. 2.

    If X=ℂ​ℙmX=\mathds{CP}^{m} then (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies correspond to eigenfamilies of homogeneous U⁡(1)U(1)-invariant complex valued polynomials on ℂm+1\mathds{C}^{m+1}. The algebra of U⁡(1)U(1)-invariant polynomials is generated by zi​zj¯z_{i}\overline{z_{j}}, where i,j∈{1,..,m+1}i,j\in\{1,..,m+1\}. Such polynomials are often called bi-invariant. The range of values (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu) for which there exist global (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies is {(−4​d​(m+d),−4​d2)∣d∈ℕ}\{(-4d(m+d),-4d^{2})\mid d\in\mathds{N}\}.

  3. 3.

    If X=ℍ​ℙmX=\mathds{HP}^{m} then (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies correspond to eigenfamilies of homogeneous S​U​(2)SU(2)-invariant complex valued polynomials on ℍm+1\mathds{H}^{m+1}. The range of values (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu) for which there exist global (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)-eigenfamilies is {(−4​d​(2​m+1+d),−4​d2)∣d∈ℕ}\{(-4d(2m+1+d),-4d^{2})\mid d\in\mathds{N}\}.

3 Relations to holomorphicity

For two smooth functions f,g:ℂm→ℂf,g:\mathds{C}^{m}\to\mathds{C} one has for all x∈ℂmx\in\mathds{C}^{m}:

(∇xf)T​∇xg\displaystyle(\nabla_{\!x}f)^{T}\nabla_{\!x}g =2​∑j=1m(∂zjf​∂z¯jg+∂zjg​∂z¯jf)​(x),\displaystyle=2\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\partial_{z_{j}}f\partial_{\bar{z}_{j}}g+\partial_{z_{j}}g\partial_{\bar{z}_{j}}f\right)(x), (8)
Δ​f​(x)\displaystyle\Delta f\,(x) =4​∑j=1m(∂zj∂z¯jf)​(x),\displaystyle=4\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\partial_{z_{j}}\partial_{\bar{z}_{j}}f)\,(x), (9)

where z1,…,zmz_{1},...,z_{m} are the standard complex coordinates on ℂm\mathds{C}^{m}. In particular a family of holomorphic functions on ℂm\mathds{C}^{m} will trivially be a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily.

Pre-composing a family of holomorphic functions on ℂm\mathds{C}^{m} with an isometry or an orthogonal projection preserves the property that the functions are a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily. As remarked in the introduction, we are mostly interested in eigenfamilies that do not arise from families of holomorphic functions in this way. For convenience we will say that families constructed in this manner are uniformly of complex type, c.f. Definition 3.1 below.

In Subsection 3.1 we give a simple geometric criterion characterising families that are uniformly of complex type, this is Theorem 3. It turns out to be useful to fix what it means for a function to be “holomorphic in some variables”, this is done in in Subsection 3.2 via the notion of an axis of holomorphy c.f. Definition 3.4. This notion is the source of much of the flexibility one has in generating examples, see also the discussion of Section 5.3.

We use the notion of an axis of holomorphy to show Theorem 4, also in Subsection 3.2. In Subsection 3.3 we briefly describe how an axis of holomorphy leads to a reduction procedure and use this to show Theorem 5.

3.1 Functions and families of complex type

Definition 3.1.
  1. 1.

    A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions from ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} said to be uniformly of complex type if there is a k≥0k\geq 0, an orthogonal projection π:ℝm→ℂk\pi:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}^{k}, and a family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of holomorphic maps ℂk→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\to\mathds{C} so that ℱ=π∗​(𝒢):={G∘π∣G∈𝒢}\mathcal{F}=\pi^{*}(\mathcal{G})\vcentcolon=\{G\circ\pi\mid G\in\mathcal{G}\}.

  2. 2.

    A function F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is said to be of complex type if the family {F}\{F\} is uniformly of complex type.

If mm is even then a function is of complex type if and only if it is congruent to a holomorphic map, i.e. differs from a holomorphic map only by an isometry of the domain. This is equivalent to the existence of a Kähler structure JJ on (ℝm,geuc)(\mathds{R}^{m},g_{\textrm{euc}}) with respect to which the map is holomorphic11 1 Recall that the complex unit of a Kähler structure is parallel.. If mm is odd, then maps of complex type on ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} factor through an even dimensional subspace, on which the above remark applies.

We briefly recall what it means for a subspace of a vector space to be isotropic:

Definition 3.2.

A complex linear subspace V⊆ℝm⊗ℂV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m}\otimes\mathds{C} is called isotropic if vT​w=0v^{T}w=0 for all v,w∈Vv,w\in V.

Theorem 3.

A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of smooth functions from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C} is uniformly of complex type if and only if the gradients {∇xF∣x∈ℝm,F∈ℱ}\{\nabla_{\!x}F\mid x\in\mathds{R}^{m},F\in\mathcal{F}\} span an isotropic subspace of ℝm⊗ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\otimes\mathds{C}, i.e. if and only if for all F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} and x,y∈ℝmx,y\in\mathds{R}^{m}:

(∇xF)T​∇yG=0.(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!y}G=0. (10)
Proof.

If ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type then, as remarked before, we may assume the domain to be ℂk\mathds{C}^{k} and each F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} to be holomorphic. Equation (10) is then a direct consequence of the Cauchy-Riemann equations, recall equation (8).

On the other hand, if equation (10) holds, then V:=spanℂ{∇xF∣x∈ℝm,F∈ℱ}V\vcentcolon=\mathrm{span}_{\mathds{C}}\{\nabla_{\!x}F\mid x\in\mathds{R}^{m},F\in\mathcal{F}\} is an isotropic subspace of ℝm⊗ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\otimes\mathds{C}. Let z1,…,zkz_{1},...,z_{k} be an orthonormal basis of VV with respect to the usual Hermitian inner product on ℝm⊗ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\otimes\mathds{C}. For every j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,...,k\}, define xj,yj∈ℝmx_{j},y_{j}\in\mathds{R}^{m} via:

zj=12​(xj+i​yj).z_{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x_{j}+iy_{j}).

Since the vectors zjz_{j} are isotropic, orthogonal and of norm 11, it follows that x1,…,xk,y1,…,ykx_{1},...,x_{k},y_{1},...,y_{k} constitute an orthonormal system of ℝm\mathds{R}^{m}. Define:

a:ℂk→ℝm,(λ1,…,λk)↦∑j=1kRe⁡(λj)​xj+∑j=1kIm⁡(λj)​yj,a:\mathds{C}^{k}\to\mathds{R}^{m},\qquad(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{k})\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_{j})x_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathrm{Im}(\lambda_{j})y_{j},

which is then isometric and ℝ\mathds{R}-linear. We take π=a∗\pi=a^{*} to be the adjoint of aa and let 𝒢={F∘a∣F∈ℱ}\mathcal{G}=\{F\circ a\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\}.

We now check that F∘(a​a∗)=FF\circ(aa^{*})=F and that F∘aF\circ a is holomorphic for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. Note that a​a∗:ℝm→ℝmaa^{*}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{m} is an orthogonal projection to the image of aa. Suppose that v∈ℝmv\in\mathds{R}^{m} with v⟂a⁡(ℂk)v\perp a(\mathds{C}^{k}). Then we have for all z∈ℝmz\in\mathds{R}^{m}:

dd​t​F​(z+t​v)=(∇z+t​vF)T⋅v=∑j=1kλj​(t)​zjT​v=∑j=1kλj​(t)​(xjT​v+i​yjT​v)=0\frac{d}{dt}F(z+tv)=(\nabla_{\!z+tv}F)^{T}\cdot v=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}(t)z_{j}^{T}v=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}(t)(x_{j}^{T}v+iy_{j}^{T}v)=0

where we have decomposed ∇z+t​vF=∑jλj​(t)​zj\nabla_{z+tv}F=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}(t)z_{j} for some λj​(t)∈ℂ\lambda_{j}(t)\in\mathds{C}, this is possible since the gradient can be written as a complex linear combination of z1,…,zkz_{1},...,z_{k}. This implies F∘a​a∗=FF\circ aa^{*}=F. For holomorphicity consider z,v∈ℂkz,v\in\mathds{C}^{k}, write v=(λ1,…,λk)v=(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{k}), ∇a⁡(z)F=∑jμj​zj\nabla_{\!a(z)}F=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}z_{j}, and denote with JJ the complex unit of ℂk\mathds{C}^{k}, then:

Dz​(F∘a)​(J⋅v)\displaystyle D_{z}(F\circ a)(J\cdot v) =(∇a⁡(z)F)T(∑j−Im(λj)xj+Re(λj)yj)=12∑jμj(−Im(λj)+iRe(λj))\displaystyle=(\nabla_{a(z)}F)^{T}(\sum_{j}-\mathrm{Im}(\lambda_{j})x_{j}+\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_{j})y_{j})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{j}\mu_{j}(-\mathrm{Im}(\lambda_{j})+i\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_{j}))
=12​∑ji​μj​λj=i​(∇a⁡(z)F)T​a​(v)=i​Dz​(F∘a)​(v).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{j}i\mu_{j}\lambda_{j}=i(\nabla_{\!a(z)}F)^{T}a(v)=iD_{z}(F\circ a)(v).

This establishes the claim. ∎

Remark.

The short and quick version of the proof of Theorem 3 is that every isotropic subspace V⊂ℝm⊗ℂV\subset\mathds{R}^{m}{\otimes\mathds{C}} is the anti-holomorphic subspace {v+iJv∣v∈ℝm,v⟂kerJ}\{v+iJv\mid v\in\mathds{R}^{m},v\perp\ker J\} of a degenerate complex unit JJ, i.e. an anti-symmetric linear map ℝm→ℝm\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{m} with J2=−𝟙+pker⁡JJ^{2}=-\mathds{1}+p_{\ker J}, where pker⁡Jp_{\ker J} is the orthogonal projection to ker⁡J\ker J. If the gradients of a map FF are valued in such a subspace then FF factors over (ker⁡J)⟂(\ker J)^{\perp} and

dF(Jv)=(∇F)T(Jv)=−(J∇F)Tv=(i∇F)Tv=idF(v)dF(Jv)=(\nabla F)^{T}(Jv)=-(J\nabla F)^{T}v=(i\nabla F)^{T}v=i\,dF(v)

for all vv, whence FF is holomorphic with respect to JJ.

Remark.

If F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is a homogenous degree 22 polynomial, then conditions (7) and (10) coincide. Indeed, if F⁡(x)=xT​A​xF(x)=x^{T}Ax for AA a complex, symmetric m×mm\times m matrix, then:

(∇xF)T​∇xF=0​∀x⇔A2=0⇔(∇xF)T​∇yF=0​∀x,y.(\nabla_{x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{x}F=0\ \forall x\iff A^{2}=0\iff(\nabla_{x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{y}F=0\ \forall x,y.

As a consequence any homogenous degree 22 polynomial harmonic morphism ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is of complex type, which is well known22 2 It follows for example from the classification of homogeneous polynomial degree 22 harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n}, c.f. [17] and [16].. A similar calculation shows that any polynomial harmonic morphism of degree 22 from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}, not necessarily homogeneous, is of complex type.

Example 3.3.
  1. (i)

    The polynomials

    ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,v,w)↦z​v+u​w,ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,v,w)↦z​w¯−u​v¯\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},\ (z,u,v,w)\mapsto zv+uw,\qquad\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},\ (z,u,v,w)\mapsto z\overline{w}-u\overline{v}

    As a,b,c,da,b,c,d vary over ℂ\mathds{C} the family of maps given by

    ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,v,w)↦a⁡(z2​w+z​u​v¯)+b⁡(z​u​w¯−z2​v)+c⁡(u2​v¯+z​u​w)+d⁡(u2​w¯−z​u​v)\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},\qquad(z,u,v,w)\mapsto a(z^{2}w+zu\overline{v})+b(zu\overline{w}-z^{2}v)+c(u^{2}\overline{v}+zuw)+d(u^{2}\overline{w}-zuv)

    Let γ∈ℂ\gamma\in\mathds{C}, the map

    ℂ3⊕ℝ↦ℂ,((z,u,w),t)↦z2​w+2​γ​z​u​t−γ2​u2​w¯\mathds{C}^{3}\oplus\mathds{R}\mapsto\mathds{C},\qquad((z,u,w),t)\mapsto z^{2}w+2\gamma\,zut-\gamma^{2}u^{2}\overline{w}

Remark.

The analog of Theorem 3 and equation (10) to more general Riemannian manifolds (M,g)(M,g) would be as follows: Given a family ℱ\mathcal{F} one would consider the equation

gℂ​(Pγ​∇xMF,∇yMG)=0g_{\mathds{C}}(P_{\gamma}\nabla_{\!x}^{M}F,\nabla_{\!y}^{M}G)=0 (11)

for all x,y∈Mx,y\in M, F,G∈MF,G\in M and γ\gamma paths from xx to yy. Here PγP_{\gamma} denotes parallel transport. This is equivalent to all parallel translates of gradients from ℱ\mathcal{F} generating a parallel isotropic subspace of T​M⊗ℂTM\otimes\mathds{C}. By de Rahm’s Theorem the universal cover of MM is then a Riemannian product of a Kähler manifold and another Riemannian manifold. The family ℱ\mathcal{F} factors over the Kähler factor, on which it is a family of holomorphic functions.

3.2 Axis of holomorphy

In this section we briefly define what it means for a family of functions to be holomorphic in some variables. The given characterisation is geometric, i.e. it does not depend on the choice of a complex structure. We then show Theorem 4.

Definition 3.4.
  1. 1.

    Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of functions ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. A vector subspace V⊆ℝmV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m} is said to be a uniform axis of holomorphy of ℱ\mathcal{F} if the family

    {F(x+⋅):V→ℂ,v↦F(x+v)∣x∈ℝm,F∈ℱ}\{F(x+\cdot):V\to\mathds{C},v\mapsto F(x+v)\mid x\in\mathds{R}^{m},F\in\mathcal{F}\}

    is uniformly of complex type.

  2. 2.

    Let F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} be a function. A vector subspace V⊆ℝmV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m} is said to be an axis of holomorphy of FF if VV is a uniform axis of holomorphy of {F}\{F\}.

Example 3.5.

For all families listed in Example 3.3 the ℂ2\mathds{C}^{2} subspace (of the respective domains) spanned by the variables zz and uu is a uniform axis of holomorphy.

Remark.

The author does not know any examples of polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} without an axis of holomorphy. Numerics indicate that generically the degree 33 or 44 homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms on ℝ6\mathds{R}^{6} have such an axis. In particular these polynomials are generically of complex type by Theorem 5. In my opinion the question of whether or not an axis must exist is probably the most approachable question when attempting to classify polynomial harmonic morphisms to ℂ\mathds{C}. It is natural to ask:

Question 3.6.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily on ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} consisting of homogeneous polynomials. Does ℱ\mathcal{F} admit a non-trivial uniform axis of holomorphy?

We now provide some simple criterions for recognising such an axis. As an immediate consequence of Theorem 3 one sees:

Proposition 3.7.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of smooth functions from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}, and V⊆ℝmV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m} a vector subspace. Denote with pVp_{V} the orthogonal projection to VV. Then VV is a uniform axis of holomorphy of ℱ\mathcal{F} if and only if (∇xF1)T​pV​∇yF2=0(\nabla_{\!x}F_{1})^{T}p_{V}\nabla_{\!y}F_{2}=0 for all x,y∈ℝmx,y\in\mathds{R}^{m}, F1,F2∈ℱF_{1},F_{2}\in\mathcal{F}.

In particular a one-dimensional subspace V⊆ℝmV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m} is a uniform axis of holomorphy of a family ℱ\mathcal{F} if and only if pV​∇x​F=0p_{V}\nabla_{\!x}F=0 for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathds{R}^{m}, F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. This is equivalent to FF factoring over the projection to V⟂V^{\perp} for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. The case of a 22-dimensional axis is more useful and interesting:

Lemma 3.8.

Let V⊆ℝmV\subseteq\mathds{R}^{m}, dim(V)=2\dim(V)=2 and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of functions ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. Then VV is a uniform axis of holomorphy of ℱ\mathcal{F} if and only if there exists an orthonormal basis {u,v}\{u,v\} of VV so that any of the following equivalent conditions hold:

  1. (i)

    For all x∈ℝm,F∈ℱx\in\mathds{R}^{m},F\in\mathcal{F} one has (∇xF)T​(u+i​v)=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}(u+iv)=0.

  2. (ii)

    For all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} there is a λF:ℝm→ℂ\lambda_{F}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} so that for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathds{R}^{m} one has

    pV​(∇xF)=λF​(x)​(u+i​v).p_{V}(\nabla_{\!x}F)=\lambda_{F}(x)(u+iv).
Proof.

Note that (ii) clearly implies both (i) and that VV is an axis of holomorphy.

On the other hand if VV is an axis of holomorphy then either pV​(∇xF)=0p_{V}(\nabla_{\!x}F)=0 for all x,Fx,F and then (i) and (ii) follow or there are y,Qy,Q with pV​(∇yQ)≠0p_{V}(\nabla_{\!y}Q)\neq 0. Taking u~,v~\widetilde{u},\widetilde{v} to be the real and imaginary parts of pV​(∇yQ)p_{V}(\nabla_{\!y}Q) respectively, one gets from (∇yQ)T​pV​∇yQ=0(\nabla_{\!y}Q)^{T}p_{V}\nabla_{\!y}Q=0 that they have the same norm and are orthogonal to each other. Then (∇xF)T​pV​∇yQ=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}p_{V}\nabla_{\!y}Q=0 for all x,Fx,F implies (i) for u=u~‖u~‖,v=v~‖v~‖u=\frac{\widetilde{u}}{\|\widetilde{u}\|},v=\frac{\widetilde{v}}{\|\widetilde{v}\|}.

It remains to show that (i) implies (ii). But this is obvious, since u+i​v,u−i​vu+iv,u-iv are a complex basis of V⊗ℂV\otimes\mathds{C}, so there are λF,λ~F:ℝm→ℂ\lambda_{F},\widetilde{\lambda}_{F}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} with

pV​(∇xF)=λF​(x)​(u+i​v)+λ~F​(x)​(u−i​v).p_{V}(\nabla_{\!x}F)=\lambda_{F}(x)(u+iv)+\widetilde{\lambda}_{F}(x)(u-iv).

If λ~F​(x)≠0\widetilde{\lambda}_{F}(x)\neq 0 for any x,Fx,F, then (i) fails for this pair x,Fx,F. Thus λ~F=0\widetilde{\lambda}_{F}=0 for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} and (ii) follows. ∎

A result of Baird and Wood states that every globally defined harmonic morphism ℝ3→ℂ\mathds{R}^{3}\to\mathds{C} is of complex type, c.f. Theorem 4.1 in [3]. Wood [19] has shown that the same for harmonic morphisms ℝ4→ℂ\mathds{R}^{4}\to\mathds{C}, see e.g. Theorem 7.11.6 in [5]. We extend these results to (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies, using the notion of an axis of holomorphy and Lemma 3.8.

Theorem 4.

Let m≤4m\leq 4 and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily of maps (not necessarily polynomials) ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type.

Proof.

It suffices to prove the statement for m=4m=4. For F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} define VF:=spanℂ⁡{∇xF∣x∈ℝ4}V_{F}\vcentcolon=\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{\nabla_{\!x}F\mid x\in\mathds{R}^{4}\}. Then, since FF is of complex type, VFV_{F} is an isotropic subspace of ℝ4⊗ℂ\mathds{R}^{4}\otimes\mathds{C} and so dimℂ(VF)∈{0,1,2}\dim_{\mathds{C}}(V_{F})\in\{0,1,2\}. Without loss of generality we assume dimℂ(VF)≠0\dim_{\mathds{C}}(V_{F})\neq 0 for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}.

We first show that if ℱ\mathcal{F} admits a uniform axis of holomorphy of real dimension 22 that it is then uniformly of complex type.

By Lemma 3.8 the existence of such an axis is equivalent to a non-zero isotropic vector w∈ℝ4⊗ℂw\in\mathds{R}^{4}\otimes\mathds{C} so that (∇xF)T​w=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,w=0 for all x∈ℝ4,F∈ℱx\in\mathds{R}^{4},F\in\mathcal{F}. This ww annihilates all VFV_{F} and so VF+spanℂ⁡{w}V_{F}+\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{w\} is isotropic for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, it is then of dimension ≤2\leq 2. For any F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} there is then an isotropic vector w⁡(F)⟂ww(F)\perp w (possibly w⁡(F)=0w(F)=0) so that VF+spanℂ⁡{w}=spanℂ⁡{w,w⁡(F)}V_{F}+\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{w\}=\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{w,w(F)\}. For any F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} there are then functions λF,μF:ℝ4→ℂ\lambda_{F},\mu_{F}:\mathds{R}^{4}\to\mathds{C} for which:

∇xF=λF​(x)​w+μF​(x)​w​(F).\nabla_{\!x}F=\lambda_{F}(x)w+\mu_{F}(x)w(F).

The functions μF\mu_{F} can be chosen to be of complex type (since if w⁡(F)≠0w(F)\neq 0 one has μF​(x)=1‖w⁡(F)‖​(∇xF)T​w⁡(F)¯\mu_{F}(x)=\frac{1}{\|w(F)\|}(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\overline{w(F)}). In particular each such function is either non-zero on an open dense set or constant zero. Using the fact that spanℂ⁡{w,w⁡(F)}\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{w,w(F)\} is isotropic one gets for all x∈ℝ4x\in\mathds{R}^{4} and F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} that:

(∇xF)T​∇xG=μF​(x)​μG​(x)​w​(F)T​w​(G)=0,(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}G=\mu_{F}(x)\mu_{G}(x)\ w(F)^{T}w(G)=0,

implying that whenever both of μF,μG\mu_{F},\mu_{G} are not the zero function that w​(F)T​w​(G)=0w(F)^{T}w(G)=0. One then sees:

(∇xF)T​∇yG=μF​(x)​μG​(y)​w​(F)T​w​(G)=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!y}G=\mu_{F}(x)\mu_{G}(y)\,w(F)^{T}w(G)=0

for all x,y∈ℝ4,F,G∈ℱx,y\in\mathds{R}^{4},F,G\in\mathcal{F} and ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type.

For the second step we show that if there is a F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} so that dim(VF)=1\dim(V_{F})=1, that VFV_{F} is a uniform axis of holomorphy for ℱ\mathcal{F}:

There is then a non-zero isotropic vector w∈ℝ4⊗ℂw\in\mathds{R}^{4}\otimes\mathds{C} and a function λ:ℝ4→ℂ\lambda:\mathds{R}^{4}\to\mathds{C} so that ∇xF=λ⁡(x)​w\nabla_{\!x}F=\lambda(x)w. As before λ\lambda is non-zero on an open dense set, so (∇xG)T​∇xF=0(\nabla_{\!x}G)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}F=0 implies (∇xG)T​w=0(\nabla_{\!x}G)^{T}\,w=0 for all x∈ℝ4x\in\mathds{R}^{4}, G∈ℱG\in\mathcal{F}. VFV_{F} is then a uniform axis of holomorphy for ℱ\mathcal{F} by Lemma 3.8.

In the final step we suppose dimℂ(VF)=2\dim_{\mathds{C}}(V_{F})=2 for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. We then suppose that ℱ\mathcal{F} is not uniformly of complex type, i.e. that there exist x,y∈ℝ4x,y\in\mathds{R}^{4}, F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} for which:

(∇xF)T​∇yG≠0.(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!y}G\neq 0.

This will lead to a contradiction. We choose an orthonormal basis w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} of VFV_{F}, then there are functions λ1,λ2,μ1,μ2,μ3,μ4:ℝ4→ℂ\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3},\mu_{4}:\mathds{R}^{4}\to\mathds{C} so that:

∇xF=λ1​(x)​w1+λ2​(x)​w2,∇xG=μ1​(x)​w1¯+μ2​(x)​w2¯+μ3​(x)​w1+μ4​(x)​w2.\nabla_{\!x}F=\lambda_{1}(x)w_{1}+\lambda_{2}(x)w_{2},\quad\nabla_{\!x}G=\mu_{1}(x)\overline{w_{1}}+\mu_{2}(x)\overline{w_{2}}+\mu_{3}(x){w_{1}}+\mu_{4}(x)w_{2}.

The condition (∇xF)T​∇xG=0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}G=0 is then equivalent to λ1​(x)λ2​(x)=−μ2​(x)μ1​(x)\frac{\lambda_{1}(x)}{\lambda_{2}(x)}=-\frac{\mu_{2}(x)}{\mu_{1}(x)} whenever both sides are defined (which we may assume to be almost everywhere).

Since λi​(x)=(∇xF)T​wi¯\lambda_{i}(x)=(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\overline{w_{i}} the quotient λ1​(x)λ2​(x)\frac{\lambda_{1}(x)}{\lambda_{2}(x)} is holomorphic with respect to the same complex structure that makes FF holomorphic. In particular its gradient (which is not constant zero) will lie in VFV_{F}. Similarly the gradient of −μ2​(x)μ1​(x)-\frac{\mu_{2}(x)}{\mu_{1}(x)} lies in VGV_{G}. Since these two functions are however equal one has that VF∩VG≠{0}V_{F}\cap V_{G}\neq\{0\}; and so {F,G}\{F,G\} admits a uniform axis of holomorphy of (real) dimension 22. By the first step of the proof {F,G}\{F,G\} is then uniformly of complex type, contradicting the assumption that there are x,y∈ℝ4x,y\in\mathds{R}^{4} so that (∇xF)T​∇yG≠0(\nabla_{\!x}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!y}G\neq 0. ∎

3.3 Reduction along axis

In this section we remark on a reduction principle for homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms that admit an axis of holomorphy (of dimension at least 22), see Proposition 3.10. The reduction decreases the dimension of the domain while preserving the property of being a harmonic morphism, at the cost of potentially losing homogeneity.

Since (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies in dimension ≤4\leq 4 are well understood by Theorem 4, this yields Theorem 5 and Proposition 3.11.

Definition 3.9.

Let m,d∈ℕm,d\in\mathds{N} and let F:ℂ⊕ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{C}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} be a homogeneous degree dd polynomial that is holomorphic in the ℂ\mathds{C} factor. Define the reduction of FF along ℂ\mathds{C} by:

ρ⁡(F):ℝm→ℂ,x↦F⁡(1,x),\rho(F):\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C},\qquad x\mapsto F(1,x),

which is a polynomial of degree ≤d\leq d, not necessarily homogeneous.

Proposition 3.10.

Let m,d∈ℕm,d\in\mathds{N} and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of homogeneous degree dd polynomials from ℂ⊕ℝm\mathds{C}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C} that are holomorphic in the ℂ\mathds{C} factor. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is an eigenfamily if and only if {ρ⁡(F)∣F∈ℱ}\{\rho(F)\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\} is.

Proof.

For F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F} we write with respect to the decomposition ℂ⊕ℝm\mathds{C}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m}:

F⁡(z,x)=∑k=0dzd−k​Fk​(x),G⁡(z,x)=∑k=0dzd−k​Gk​(z,x)F(z,x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}z^{d-k}F_{k}(x),\qquad G(z,x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}z^{d-k}G_{k}(z,x)

where Fk,GkF_{k},G_{k} are homogeneous degree kk polynomials ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. In particular ρ⁡(F)​(x)=∑k=0dFk​(x)\rho(F)(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}F_{k}(x). Then ℱ\mathcal{F} is an eigenfamily if and only if:

(∇(z,x)F)T∇(z,x)G=∑k=22​dz2​d−k∑i,j:i+j=k(∇xFi)T∇xGj=0(\nabla_{\!(z,x)}F)^{T}\,\nabla_{\!(z,x)}G=\sum_{k=2}^{2d}z^{2d-k}\sum_{i,j:i+j=k}(\nabla_{\!x}F_{i})^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}G_{j}=0 (12)

for all (z,x)(z,x) and F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F}. On the other hand {ρ⁡(F)∣F∈ℱ}\{\rho(F)\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\} is an eigenfamily if and only if

(∇xρ(F))T(∇xρ(G))=∑k=22​d∑i,j:i+j=k(∇xFi)T∇xGj=0(\nabla_{\!x}\rho(F))^{T}\,(\nabla_{\!x}\rho(G))=\sum_{k=2}^{2d}\ \sum_{i,j:i+j=k}(\nabla_{\!x}F_{i})^{T}\,\nabla_{\!x}G_{j}=0 (13)

for all x∈ℝmx\in\mathds{R}^{m} and F,G∈ℱF,G\in\mathcal{F}. By comparing the degrees in xx one sees that equations (12), (13) are equivalent. The proposition then follows. ∎

Combining Theorem 4 with the reduction procedure then immediately yields:

Theorem 5.

Let m∈{5,6}m\in\{5,6\} and suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is an eigenfamily of homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C}. If ℱ\mathcal{F} has a uniform axis of holomorphy of (real) dimension at least 22, then ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type.

Proof.

Identifying ℝm≅ℂ⊕ℝm−2\mathds{R}^{m}\cong\mathds{C}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m-2} we may then assume the axis of holomorphy to be the ℂ\mathds{C} factor. Reducing along this axis as in Proposition 3.10 then results in a polynomial eigenfamily on ℝm−2\mathds{R}^{m-2}, which is then of complex type by Theorem 4. For each F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} one may write ρ⁡(F)=∑kFk\rho(F)=\sum_{k}F_{k} as a sum of homogeneous polynomials, all of different degrees. Since {ρ⁡(F)∣F∈ℱ}\{\rho(F)\mid F\in\mathcal{F}\} is uniformly of complex type it follows that {Fk∣k∈ℕ,F∈ℱ}\{F_{k}\mid k\in\mathds{N},F\in\mathcal{F}\} is also uniformly of complex type.

Undoing the reduction then implies that ℱ\mathcal{F} is uniformly of complex type. ∎

Remark.

The statement of Theorem 5 does not extend to non-homogeneous polynomials, as the example

ℂ2⊕ℝ→ℂ,((z,w),t)↦z2​w+2​γ​z​t−γ2​w¯\mathds{C}^{2}\oplus\mathds{R}\to\mathds{C},\qquad((z,w),t)\mapsto z^{2}w+2\gamma zt-\gamma^{2}\overline{w}

(due to Ababou, Baird, and Brossard [1]) shows, here γ∈ℂ\gamma\in\mathds{C}. Similarly it doesn’t extend to domain ℝ7\mathds{R}^{7}, as demonstrated by inflating the previous example:

ℂ3⊕ℝ→ℂ,((z,u,w),t)↦z2​w+2​γ​z​u​t−γ2​u2​w¯.\mathds{C}^{3}\oplus\mathds{R}\to\mathds{C},\qquad((z,u,w),t)\mapsto z^{2}w+2\gamma zut-\gamma^{2}u^{2}\overline{w}.

By the reduction procedure Proposition 3.10, homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} without an axis of holomorphy contain in some sense information that appears for the first time in dimension mm. Another way in which a harmonic morphism F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} might originate from a combination of lower dimensional data is if there is a decomposition ℝm=V⊕V⟂\mathds{R}^{m}=V\oplus V^{\perp} with respect to which FF is a harmonic morphism in each variable separately. This means that for all (x0,y0)∈V⊕V⟂(x_{0},y_{0})\in V\oplus V^{\perp} the maps

V→ℂ,x↦F⁡(x,y0),V⟂↦ℂ,y↦F⁡(x0,y),V\to\mathds{C},\quad x\mapsto F(x,y_{0}),\qquad V^{\perp}\mapsto\mathds{C},\quad y\mapsto F(x_{0},y),

are harmonic morphisms.

The content of the next proposition is that, in low dimensions, polynomials without an axis of holomorphy can never be written as a harmonic morphism in each variable separately.

Proposition 3.11.

Let m≤9m\leq 9 and suppose F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism not admitting a non-trivial axis of holomorphy. Then there is no non-trivial decomposition ℝm≅V⊕V⟂\mathds{R}^{m}\cong V\oplus V^{\perp} with respect to which FF is a harmonic morphism in each variable separately.

Proof.

Suppose ℝm=V⊕V⟂\mathds{R}^{m}=V\oplus V^{\perp} is a decomposition with respect to which FF is a harmonic morphism in each variable separately. Without loss of generality we assume dim(V)∈{1,2,3,4}\dim(V)\in\{1,2,3,4\}. We then find for k∈{0,..,deg(F)}k\in\{0,..,\deg(F)\} homogeneous polynomials Ak:V→ℂA_{k}:V\to\mathds{C}, Bk:V⟂→ℂB_{k}:V^{\perp}\to\mathds{C} of degree kk so that for (x,y)∈V⊕V⟂(x,y)\in V\oplus V^{\perp}:

F⁡(x,y)=∑k=0deg⁡(F)Ak​(x)​Bdeg⁡(F)−k​(y).F(x,y)=\sum_{k=0}^{\deg(F)}A_{k}(x)B_{\deg(F)-k}(y).

Without loss of generality we may assume that none of the maps B0,…,Bdeg⁡(P)B_{0},...,B_{\deg(P)} are identically zero, then there is a y0∈V⟂y_{0}\in V^{\perp} so that Bk​(y0)≠0B_{k}(y_{0})\neq 0 holds simultaneously for all kk. Since FF is a harmonic morphism in both variables separately one gets that the map

V→ℂ,x↦∑k=0deg⁡(F)Ak​(x)​Bdeg⁡(P)−k​(y0)V\to\mathds{C},\qquad x\mapsto\sum_{k=0}^{\deg(F)}A_{k}(x)B_{\deg(P)-k}(y_{0})

is a harmonic morphism. Since dim(V)≤4\dim(V)\leq 4 it is of complex type. Then the summands {A1,…,Adeg⁡(F)}\{A_{1},...,A_{\deg(F)}\} (which are all of different degrees) are uniformly of complex type. It follows that VV is an axis of holomorphy of FF, which was not permitted. ∎

4 Eigenfamilies of degree 22

In this section we discuss eigenfamilies consisting of homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms of degree 22. We begin by showing that any such family must have a uniform axis of holomorphy of dimension at least 22.

Subsections 4.1 and 4.2 then deal with the classification of pairs of homogeneous degree 22 polynomials {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} that constitute an eigenfamily, see Theorem 7.

Theorem 6.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an eigenfamily of homogeneous degree 22 polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. Then ℱ\mathcal{F} admits a uniform axis of holomorphy of (real) dimension at least min⁡(2,m)\min(2,m).

Proof.

Let A1,..,AkA_{1},..,A_{k} be symmetric matrices so that the maps x↦xT​Aj​xx\mapsto x^{T}A_{j}x, j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,...,k\} form a basis of spanℂ⁡(ℱ)\spn_{\mathds{C}}(\mathcal{F}). Note that ℱ\mathcal{F} being an eigenfamily is equivalent to

Ai​Aj+Aj​Ai=0A_{i}A_{j}+A_{j}A_{i}=0

for all i,j∈{1,…,k}i,j\in\{1,...,k\}, including i=ji=j.

Let Ai1⋯Aiℓ≠0A_{i_{1}}\cdots A_{i_{\ell}}\neq 0 be so that Aj(Ai1⋯Aiℓ)=0A_{j}(A_{i_{1}}\cdots A_{i_{\ell}})=0 for all j∈{1,…,k}j\in\{1,...,k\}. By the anti-commutator relation above such a product exists. If ℓ≠0\ell\neq 0 then the range of Ai1⋯AiℓA_{i_{1}}\cdots A_{i_{\ell}} is non-zero and consists of isotropic vectors that annihilate all of the AjA_{j}, by Lemma 3.8 ℱ\mathcal{F} then admits an axis of holomorphy of real dimension 22. If ℓ=0\ell=0 then all of the AjA_{j} vanish and the theorem follows anyway. ∎

4.1 Degree 22 eigenfamilies with 22 elements

Definition 4.1.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of smooth functions ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}. A uniform axis of holomorphy VV of ℱ\mathcal{F} is called maximal if it is not contained in any other uniform axis of holomorphy.

It is clear that any family of functions ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} admits a maximal uniform axis of holomorphy, and that the dimension of this axis is always the same.

For economy of notation we will assume all families to be full:

Definition 4.2.

A family ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is called full if there is no proper subspace V⊂ℝmV\subset\mathds{R}^{m} so that F=F∘pVF=F\circ p_{V} for all F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}, where pV:ℝm→ℝmp_{V}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{m} denotes the orthogonal projection to VV.

In this section we provide a classification of all pairs F1,F2:ℝm→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} of homogenous degree 22 polynomials so that {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} is an eigenfamily. To this end we introduce some notation:

Definition 4.3.
  1. 1.

    We call a triple (n,k,δ)(n,k,\delta) of natural numbers a subspace type if n≥kn\geq k, kk is even, and δ∈{0,1}\delta\in\{0,1\}.

  2. 2.

    We call a triple (P1,P2,A)(P_{1},P_{2},A) polynomial data of a subspace type (n,k,δ)(n,k,\delta) if P1,P2∈ℂ⁡[z1,…,zn]P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathds{C}[z_{1},...,z_{n}] are homogenous complex polynomials of degree 22 and AA is a complex n×kn\times k matrix of rank kk.

  3. 3.

    We call a triple (Y,C,v)(Y,C,v) twisting data of a subspace type (n,k,δ)(n,k,\delta) if Y,CY,C are anti-symmetric k×kk\times k matrices, YY is invertible, and if v∈ℂkv\in\mathds{C}^{k} with v=0v=0 if and only if δ=0\delta=0.

Theorem 7.

Let F1,F2:ℝm→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} be two homogenous degree 22 polynomials so that {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} is a full eigenfamily. Then there are subspace data (n,k,δ)(n,k,\delta) as well as polynomial and twisting data (P1,P2,A)(P_{1},P_{2},A), (Y,C,v)(Y,C,v) so that:

  1. 1.

    Up to an isometry of the domain one can decompose ℝm≅ℂn⊕ℂk⊕ℝδ\mathds{R}^{m}\cong\mathds{C}^{n}\oplus\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{\delta} so that ℂn\mathds{C}^{n} is a maximal uniform axis of holomorphy for {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\}.

  2. 2.

    Let X=(12​v​vT+C)​Y−1X=(\frac{1}{2}vv^{T}+C)Y^{-1}. One has, with respect to the above decomposition:

    F1((z1,….,zn),(w1,…,wk),t)\displaystyle F_{1}((z_{1},....,z_{n}),(w_{1},...,w_{k}),t) =P1​(z1,…,zn)+∑i​jzi​Ai​j​wj\displaystyle=P_{1}(z_{1},...,z_{n})+\sum_{ij}z_{i}A_{ij}w_{j}
    F2((z1,….,zn),(w1,…,wk),t)\displaystyle F_{2}((z_{1},....,z_{n}),(w_{1},...,w_{k}),t) =P2​(z1,…,zn)+∑i​jzi​Ai​j​(∑lXj​l​wl+∑lYj​l​w¯l+vj​t)\displaystyle=P_{2}(z_{1},...,z_{n})+\sum_{ij}z_{i}A_{ij}\left(\sum_{l}X_{jl}w_{l}+\sum_{l}Y_{jl}\overline{w}_{l}+v_{j}t\right)

Additionally for any subspace type together with polynomial and twisting data the above equations define an eigenfamily on ℝ2​(n+k)+δ\mathds{R}^{2(n+k)+\delta}.

Example 4.4.

The following are minimal non-trivial examples of such eigenpairs:

  1. (i)

    F1,F2:ℂ4→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C} given by

    F1​(z,u,v,w)=z​v+u​w,F2​(z,u,v,w)=z​w¯−z​v¯.F_{1}(z,u,v,w)=zv+uw,\qquad F_{2}(z,u,v,w)=z\overline{w}-z\overline{v}.

    Here

    (n,k,δ)=(2,2,0),(P1,P2,A)=(0,0,(1001)),(Y,C,v)=((01−10),0,0).(n,k,\delta)=(2,2,0),\quad(P_{1},P_{2},A)=(0,0,\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}),\quad(Y,C,v)=(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix},0,0).
  2. (ii)

    F1,F2:ℂ4⊕ℝ→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{C}^{4}\oplus\mathds{R}\to\mathds{C} given by

    F1​(z,u,v,w,t)=z​v+u​w,F2​(z,u,v,w,t)=z⁡(w¯+w+2​i​t)−u​v¯.F_{1}(z,u,v,w,t)=zv+uw,\qquad F_{2}(z,u,v,w,t)=z(\overline{w}+w+2it)-u\overline{v}.

    Here δ=1\delta=1 and v=(20)v=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, the other data are as in the previous example.

Remark.

More generally if M1,…,MkM_{1},...,M_{k} are symmetric complex m×mm\times m matrices one notes that the the maps x↦xT​Mi​xx\mapsto x^{T}M_{i}x form a degree 22 (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily iff and only if

{Mi,Mj}=0​∀i,j.\{M_{i},M_{j}\}=0\ \forall i,j.

This is the same data as a representation of the exterior algebra ρ:Λ⁡(ℂk)→End⁡(ℝm)\rho:\Lambda(\mathds{C}^{k})\to\End(\mathds{R}^{m}) for which the generators Λ1​(ℂk)\Lambda^{1}(\mathds{C}^{k}) are sent to symmetric matrices. This is superficially similar to the case for quadratic harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n}, which can be classified via the theory of orthogonal representations of Clifford algebras, which is particularly simple. However unlike the Clifford algebras the exterior algebra Λ⁡(ℂk)\Lambda(\mathds{C}^{k}) is wild if k≥3k\geq 3 (since it contains a wild quotient, cf. e.g. [18]). Since the representation theory of wild algebras is generally regarded as an impossible problem one is unlikely to profit from this approach.

Remark.

The previous remark does not mean that the classification of e.g. degree 22 homogeneous (0,0)(0,0)-eigentriples {P,Q,O}\{P,Q,O\} should be regarded as impossible. As an example the free algebra of two generators is wild, but its representations are easily parametrised by two matrices. It is the problem of classifying the indecomposable representations that is hard.

4.2 Proof of Theorem 7

Let F1,F2:ℝm→ℂF_{1},F_{2}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} be two homogenous polynomials of degree 22 so that {F1,F2}\{F_{1},F_{2}\} is full. F2​((z1,…,zn),(w1,…,wk),t)=P2​(z)+∑i​jzi​Ai​j​(∑lXj​l​wl+∑lYj​l​wl¯+vj​t)F_{2}((z_{1},...,z_{n}),(w_{1},...,w_{k}),t)=P_{2}(z)+\sum_{ij}z_{i}A_{ij}(\sum_{l}X_{jl}w_{l}+\sum_{l}Y_{jl}\overline{w_{l}}+v_{j}t)

5 Constructions of polynomial eigenfamilies

This section details some ways in which eigenfamilies of homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphims from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℂ\mathds{C} may be constructed.

5.1 Eigenfamilies induced by polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n}

Harmonic morphisms from ℝm\mathds{R}^{m} to ℝn\mathds{R}^{n} that are polynomial in each component have been studied before. While Eells and Yiu [7] find all such polynomials that restrict to a map of spheres Sm−1→Sn−1S^{m-1}\to S^{n-1}, and all homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} of degree 22 are classified by the works of Ou and Wood [16, 17], not so much is known about higher degree polynomials. Ababou, Baird, and Brossard [1] derive restrictions on the dimensions of domain and codomain of a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism, and show that the symbol at a critical point of a weakly horizontal map between two Riemannian manifolds Mm→NnM^{m}\to N^{n} gives a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n}. See chapter 5 of [5] for a unified treatment.

One checks the following elementary property of harmonic morphisms with codomain ℝn\mathds{R}^{n}, see e.g. [5]:

Lemma 5.1.

A map P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} is a harmonic morphism if and only if for all j,k∈{1,…,n}j,k\in\{1,...,n\}, j≠kj\neq k the map Pj+i​Pk:ℝm→ℂP_{j}+iP_{k}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is a harmonic morphism.

It then immediately follows:

Proposition 5.2.

If P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} is a harmonic morphism then the family of functions

ℰ⁡(P):={P2​k−1+i​P2​k|k∈{1,…,⌊n2⌋}}\mathcal{E}(P)\vcentcolon=\left\{P_{2k-1}+iP_{2k}\ \middle|\ k\in\{1,...,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\}\right\}

is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily.

In particular if P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} is a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism then ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) is an eigenfamily of homogeneous polynomials.

Example 5.3.

Let P:ℍ3→ℍ,(q1,q2,q3)↦q1⋅q2⋅q3P:\mathds{H}^{3}\to\mathds{H},(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})\mapsto q_{1}\cdot q_{2}\cdot q_{3} be the multiplication of three quaternions. This is a harmonic morphism and upon identifying ℍ3≅ℂ6\mathds{H}^{3}\cong\mathds{C}^{6}, ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) is a degree 33 eigenfamily consisting of the following two maps:

ℂ6→ℂ,(z1,z2,u1,u2,w1,w2)↦z1​(u1​w1−u2​w2¯)−z2​(u1​w2¯+u2¯​w1),\displaystyle\mathds{C}^{6}\to\mathds{C},\quad(z_{1},z_{2},u_{1},u_{2},w_{1},w_{2})\mapsto z_{1}(u_{1}w_{1}-u_{2}\overline{w_{2}})-z_{2}(\overline{u_{1}w_{2}}+\overline{u_{2}}w_{1}),
ℂ6→ℂ,(z1,z2,u1,u2,w1,w2)↦z1​(u1​w2+u2​w1¯)+z2​(u1​w1¯−u2¯​w2).\displaystyle\mathds{C}^{6}\to\mathds{C},\quad(z_{1},z_{2},u_{1},u_{2},w_{1},w_{2})\mapsto z_{1}(u_{1}w_{2}+u_{2}\overline{w_{1}})+z_{2}(\overline{u_{1}w_{1}}-\overline{u_{2}}w_{2}).

Note that if B∈O⁡(n)B\in O(n) and P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} is a harmonic morphism then B∘PB\circ P is also a harmonic morphism. It may be interesting to investigate when ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) and ℰ⁡(B∘P)\mathcal{E}(B\circ P) give different eigenfamilies. For convenience we define:

Definition 5.4.

Let ℱ1,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2} be two eigenfamilies of maps ℝm→ℂ\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}, we say that ℱ1,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2} are congruent if there is an isometry Φ:ℝm→ℝm\Phi:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{m} so that

spanℂ⁡ℱ1=spanℂ⁡Φ∗​(ℱ2),\spn_{\mathds{C}}\mathcal{F}_{1}=\spn_{\mathds{C}}\Phi^{*}(\mathcal{F}_{2}),

where Φ∗​(ℱ2):={F∘Φ∣F∈ℱ2}\Phi^{*}(\mathcal{F}_{2})\vcentcolon=\{F\circ\Phi\mid F\in\mathcal{F}_{2}\}.

Using the classification of homogeneous degree 22 polynomial harmonic morphisms ℝm→ℝn\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} one can make the following observations:

Theorem 8.

Let P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} be a non-zero homogeneous degree 22 polynomial harmonic morphism.

  1. 1.

    If n≥4n\geq 4 then ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) is not uniformly of complex type.

  2. 2.

    For any B∈O⁡(n)B\in O(n) the families ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) and ℰ⁡(B∘P)\mathcal{E}(B\circ P) are congruent.

Proof.

We show point 2 first. From the classification of such maps via weighted direct sums of irreducible Clifford systems, one sees that if n≢1​mod​ 4n\not\equiv 1\,\text{mod}\,4, that there is an isometry A∈O⁡(m)A\in O(m) so that B∘P=P∘AB\circ P=P\circ A, implying that ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) and ℰ⁡(B∘P)\mathcal{E}(B\circ P) are congruent. This follows since any two irreducible representations of the Clifford algebra CnC_{n} by symmetric matrices are algebraically equivalent in this case, see e.g. Chapter 5 [5].

For the case n≡1​mod​ 4n\equiv 1\,\text{mod}\,4 let π:ℝn→ℝn−1\pi:\mathds{R}^{n}\to\mathds{R}^{n-1} denote the projection to the first n−1n-1 components. Then, since nn is odd, ℰ⁡(P)=ℰ⁡(π∘P)\mathcal{E}(P)=\mathcal{E}(\pi\circ P) and ℰ⁡(B∘P)=ℰ⁡(π∘B∘P)\mathcal{E}(B\circ P)=\mathcal{E}(\pi\circ B\circ P). Decomposing PP and B∘PB\circ P as a weighted sum of irreducible Clifford systems. One notes that the weights appearing in both decompositions must be the same (counted with multiplicity), although the irreducible representation associated to any weight may be different. It is elementary to check that the weights appearing in the Clifford decompositions of π∘P\pi\circ P and π∘B∘P\pi\circ B\circ P will be the same as those appearing in PP and B∘PB\circ P, using again that any two irreducible Clifford systems on ℝn−1\mathds{R}^{n-1} are algebraically equivalent one sees that ℰ⁡(π∘P)\mathcal{E}(\pi\circ P) and ℰ⁡(π∘B∘P)\mathcal{E}(\pi\circ B\circ P) are congruent.

For the first point let π4:ℝn→ℝ4\pi_{4}:\mathds{R}^{n}\to\mathds{R}^{4} denote the projection to the first 44 components, then π4∘P:ℝm→ℝ4\pi_{4}\circ P:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{4} is a harmonic morphism. Since ℰ⁡(π4∘P)\mathcal{E}(\pi_{4}\circ P) is a subfamily of ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P), it suffices to check that the statement in the case n=4n=4. As before PP is a weighted direct sum of irreducible Clifford systems, so it suffices to check the statement for one such summand. In this case this amounts to checking that the map ℍ⊕ℍ→ℍ\mathds{H}\oplus\mathds{H}\to\mathds{H} given by multiplication of two quaternions does not induce a family of complex type. Since the resulting family is in fact congruent to the one spanned by Example 3.3 (i), the remaining step follows.∎

This observation for degree 22 leads to the natural questions:

Question 5.5.

Let P:ℝm→ℝnP:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{R}^{n} be a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism of degree deg⁡(P)≥2\deg(P)\geq 2, and suppose n≥4n\geq 4.

  1. 1.

    Is ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) not of uniformly complex type?

  2. 2.

    Are the families ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) and ℰ⁡(B∘P)\mathcal{E}(B\circ P) congruent for all B∈O⁡(n)B\in O(n)?

5.2 Complex defects

Definition 5.6.

Let F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} and let y∈ℝmy\in\mathds{R}^{m}, the complex defect of FF at yy is the map

[F]y:ℝm→ℂ,x↦(∇xF)​∇yF.[F]_{y}:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C},\qquad x\mapsto(\nabla_{\!x}F)\nabla_{\!y}F.
Remark.

[F]y=0[F]_{y}=0 for all y∈ℝmy\in\mathds{R}^{m} if and only if FF is of complex type.

The motivation for considering this definition is the following statement, which follows e.g. from the proof of Theorem 2.1 in [1]:

Proposition 5.7.

Suppose F:ℝm→ℂF:\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} is a homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphism of degree 33. Then for all y∈ℝmy\in\mathds{R}^{m} the defects [F]y[F]_{y} are homogeneous polynomial harmonic morphisms of degree 22.

It is not necessarily the case that the defect of a higher degree harmonic morphism is again a harmonic morphism, let alone an eigenfamily. Nevertheless it works out in the following example:

Example 5.8.

Consider

P:ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,v,w)↦z2​v​w−u2​v​w¯+z​u​(|v|2−|w|2),P:\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},\qquad(z,u,v,w)\mapsto z^{2}vw-u^{2}\overline{vw}+zu(|v|^{2}-|w|^{2}),

which is a degree 44 harmonic morphism. Then the complex defects {[P]y∣y∈ℂ4}\{[P]_{y}\mid y\in\mathds{C}^{4}\} constitute an eigenfamily of degree 33 harmonic morphisms and spanℂ⁡{[P]y∣y∈ℂ4}\spn_{\mathds{C}}\{[P]_{y}\mid y\in\mathds{C}^{4}\} is given by all functions of the form

a⁡(z2​w+z​u​v¯)+b⁡(z​u​w¯−z2​v)+c⁡(u2​v¯+z​u​w)+d⁡(u2​w¯−z​u​v),a(z^{2}w+zu\overline{v})+b(zu\overline{w}-z^{2}v)+c(u^{2}\overline{v}+zuw)+d(u^{2}\overline{w}-zuv),

where a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mathds{C}. Note that such a function is of complex type if and only if a​d−b​c=0ad-bc=0.

5.3 Gluing and augmenting along an axis of holomorphy

We now give two observations on how an axis of holomorphy can be used to expand eigenfamilies and to generate new eigenfamilies. The proofs are trivial and so we omit them:

Proposition 5.9.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily of functions from ℂk⊕ℝm→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C} which are holomorphic in the ℂk\mathds{C}^{k} factor. For any family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of holomorphic functions ℂk→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\to\mathds{C} and π:ℂk⊕ℝm→ℂk\pi:\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m}\to\mathds{C}^{k} the orthogonal projection one has that

spanℂ⁡(ℱ)+spanℂ⁡(π∗​𝒢)\spn_{\mathds{C}}(\mathcal{F})+\spn_{\mathds{C}}(\pi^{*}\mathcal{G})

is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily.

Example 5.10.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the family on ℂ4\mathds{C}^{4} spanned by

ℂ4→ℂ,(z,u,v,w)↦a⁡(z2​w+z​u​v¯)+b⁡(z​u​w¯−z2​v)+c⁡(u2​v¯+z​u​w)+d⁡(u2​w¯−z​u​v)\mathds{C}^{4}\to\mathds{C},\quad(z,u,v,w)\mapsto a(z^{2}w+zu\overline{v})+b(zu\overline{w}-z^{2}v)+c(u^{2}\overline{v}+zuw)+d(u^{2}\overline{w}-zuv)

where a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mathds{C}. Denote by ℂ​[z,u]3\mathds{C}[z,u]_{3} the homogeneous degree 33 polynomials in z,uz,u, then

ℱ⊕ℂ​[z,u]3\mathcal{F}\oplus\mathds{C}[z,u]_{3}

is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily consisting of homogeneous degree 33 polynomials.

Proposition 5.11.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily ℂk⊕ℝm1→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m_{1}}\to\mathds{C} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily ℂk⊕ℝm2→ℂ\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m_{2}}\to\mathds{C}, both holomorphic in the ℂk\mathds{C}^{k} factors. Then the following is a (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamily on ℂk⊕ℝm1⊕ℝm2\mathds{C}^{k}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m_{1}}\oplus\mathds{R}^{m_{2}}:

{(z,x,y)↦P⁡(z,x)∣P∈ℱ}∪{(z,x,y)↦Q⁡(z,y)∣Q∈𝒢}.\{(z,x,y)\mapsto P(z,x)\mid P\in\mathcal{F}\}\cup\{(z,x,y)\mapsto Q(z,y)\mid Q\in\mathcal{G}\}.
Example 5.12.

Let P,Q:ℂ2⊕ℂ2→ℂP,Q:\mathds{C}^{2}\oplus\mathds{C}^{2}\to\mathds{C} be given by P⁡(z,u,v,w)=z​v+u​wP(z,u,v,w)=zv+uw, Q⁡(z,u,v,w)=z​w¯−u​v¯Q(z,u,v,w)=z\overline{w}-u\overline{v}, ℱ=𝒢={P,Q}\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{G}=\{P,Q\}. Gluing these as in Proposition 5.11 gives an eigenfamily on ℂ6\mathds{C}^{6} spanned by the functions:

P1​(z,u,v1​w1,v2,w2)=z​v1+u​w1,\displaystyle P_{1}(z,u,v_{1}w_{1},v_{2},w_{2})=zv_{1}+uw_{1}, Q1​(z,u,v1​w1,v2,w2)=z​w1¯−u​v1¯,\displaystyle Q_{1}(z,u,v_{1}w_{1},v_{2},w_{2})=z\overline{w_{1}}-u\overline{v_{1}},
P2​(z,u,v1​w1,v2,w2)=z​v2+u​w2,\displaystyle P_{2}(z,u,v_{1}w_{1},v_{2},w_{2})=zv_{2}+uw_{2}, Q2​(z,u,v1​w1,v2,w2)=z​w2¯−u​v2¯.\displaystyle Q_{2}(z,u,v_{1}w_{1},v_{2},w_{2})=z\overline{w_{2}}-u\overline{v_{2}}.
Remark.

Taking powers of (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies and Propositions 5.9, 5.11 are methods with which one can easily generate large amounts of (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies from previously known ones. It seems however quite difficult to find new (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies that do not arise in this way from known families. This suggests that the question of classifying polynomial (0,0)(0,0)-eigenfamilies has some rigidity, which should be most visible in low dimensions and degrees.
